stories.headline: Obama's lengthy reaction to Omar investigation triggers instant backlash: 'Spare me'
stories.note: Obama's long defense of Ilhan Omar amid the federal probe drew instant ridicule, tying Democrats' biggest name to a scandal-plagued congresswoman.
body: Former President Barack Obama posted a long defense of Rep. Ilhan Omar on Sunday, as the Minnesota Democrat faces federal investigations into her immigration status and her finances.
Obama called the Trump administration's handling of Omar "appalling" and argued she is being singled out because she criticizes the president. The post was viewed more than 5 million times.

Conservatives answered fast, pointing to the IRS scrutiny of Tea Party groups and the Crossfire Hurricane probe of Trump's 2016 campaign under Obama's watch. Commentator Gunther Eagleman summed it up: "Spare me the lecture, Barack."

The White House pushed back too, with spokeswoman Lauren Bis saying Trump has not used the Justice Department against his opponents. Trump has said the matter is up to the DOJ. Sources told Fox that investigators are looking at whether Omar or her father committed fraud on immigration paperwork, and D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office is examining her financial disclosures after a raid on her Washington home last week.
Omar's office called the raid an abuse of power and said she has done nothing wrong.

Why it matters: Obama is tying the party's most popular figure to a congresswoman under federal investigation, and conservatives are using his own record to call it hypocrisy just weeks before the midterms.

stories.headline: Epstein-linked billionaire pours $500K into super PAC backing Kentucky Democrat: 'Dirty Epstein-class money'
stories.note: A $500K check from an Epstein-linked billionaire to a pro-Democrat super PAC hands Republicans a ready-made attack in Kentucky.
body: LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman gave $500,000 on Sept. 24 to Kentuckians Not Corruption, a super PAC backing Democrat Zach Dembo in Kentucky's 6th Congressional District, according to FEC records.

After the donation, the group's weekly TV buys on Lexington's WLEX-TV jumped from $14,650 in mid-September to $109,990 for the week of Oct. 6, more than seven times as much. Kentucky Public Radio reported the PAC had spent about $1.6 million in the race by mid-October.

Republican nominee Ralph Alvarado, a former state senator, called it "dirty Epstein class money" and pointed to Hoffman's documented ties to Jeffrey Epstein, including visits to Epstein's island and town house.

Alvarado also called Dembo a hypocrite, since Dembo has made fighting the influence of the ultra-wealthy and dark money a centerpiece of his campaign. The article notes the money went to an independent super PAC, and records don't show Dembo asked for it.
Why it matters: Democrats hope to flip the Lexington-area seat Andy Barr is leaving to run for Senate, and the Hoffman money gives Republicans a sharp contrast to Dembo's anti-billionaire message.

stories.headline: Slotkin wants GOP prosecutions to deter young people from Trump administration jobs
stories.note: Sen. Elissa Slotkin's talk of prosecutions to scare young people away from Trump jobs feeds the GOP case that Democrats want payback.
body: Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan is taking heat for saying at an Oct. 13 University of Chicago event that she wants prosecutions to make young people think twice about working for the Trump administration.
Slotkin said she wants "signature cases" aimed not only at the president but at the people who "enabled him," and said she wants a "deterrence message" for recent graduates weighing those jobs.

Law professor Jonathan Turley said she had "said the quiet part out loud." Office of Personnel Management director Scott Kupor called the remarks disappointing and unprofessional, and said his agency wants to recruit top early-career talent.
University of Chicago student Michael Bicksel said the comments told conservative students they should fear persecution for serving their country, and vowed they won't be intimidated.
Critics also noted the remarks landed the same weekend Obama accused the Trump administration of targeting Rep. Ilhan Omar for her views.
Why it matters: With the midterms close, Slotkin's comments hand Republicans a clear example of how Democrats might use power if they win the House or Senate.

stories.headline: Pro-Israel leader warns Democrats failing to condemn 'vicious Jew haters' in Congress
stories.note: A prominent pro-Israel leader says Democrats won't police antisemitism in their own ranks, widening a rift Republicans keep exploiting.
body: Zionist Organization of America president Morton Klein, speaking for himself, told Fox News Digital that Democratic leaders have failed to forcefully condemn antisemitism among their own elected officials.
Klein named Reps. Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib, Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. He called Omar "one of the most vicious Jew haters in America."

He pointed to El-Sayed's refusal during a debate to name Iran as a bigger threat than Israel, and criticized Chuck Schumer, Sen. Elissa Slotkin and Michigan AG Dana Nessel for endorsing him anyway. He also faulted Mamdani for declining to condemn the phrase "globalize the intifada."
The article notes El-Sayed has called Judaism "a light unto the world" and pledged to protect Jewish safety, and that Mamdani has promised to fight antisemitism.
Klein also warned that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could be hemmed in if he needs left-of-center partners after Israel's Oct. 27 elections.
Why it matters: The charge that Democrats won't police their own ranks keeps pressure on the party's leaders in Michigan and beyond as the midterms approach.

stories.headline: Booker rival who 'shoots from the hip' hopes viral debate moment can break GOP's Senate drought
stories.note: Cory Booker's Republican challenger is riding a viral debate moment in a bid to end the GOP's long Senate losing streak in New Jersey.
body: Justin Murphy, a Navy veteran, attorney and former deputy mayor of Tabernacle, New Jersey, is hoping a viral moment from his debate with Sen. Cory Booker can end the GOP's long Senate drought in the state.

Asked about strategy in the Iran war, Murphy bluntly said President Trump should "finish it," a line that took off on social media. He says the answer wasn't planned and that he has no speechwriter or teleprompter.
New Jersey hasn't elected a Republican senator since Clifford Case in 1972. Murphy argues it's time for a change after Booker's 13 years in office, and says Booker can't keep blaming Trump.

He also hit Democrats over calls to dismantle the Department of Homeland Security, called election integrity critically important given noncitizen voting found in the state, and slammed Trenton's immigration stance as "utter insanity."
Booker's campaign did not respond to Fox's request for comment.
Why it matters: A blue-state challenger getting national attention on national security gives Republicans a long-shot opening in a seat Democrats usually take for granted.
